newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Matav to invest $300-$400 mln a year until 2000.
newsitem.headline: Matav to invest $300-$400 mln a year until 2000.

text.p: Hungary's telecommunication company Matav Rt will maintain its annual investment rate of $300 million to $400 million over the next few years, company officials said on Wednesday.
"The level of investment will stay up for the next two to three years but the focus will change," Ray Stewart, Matav's chief financial officer, told a news conference.

In 1996 Matav invested 70 billion forints mainly in new lines and exchanges while this year it will invest roughly the same amount but will have to build fewer new lines, another company official said.
"Last year we installed 300,000 new lines while this year's plan calls for 200,000 new lines," said Elek Straub, Matav's president and CEO.

Matav said its preliminary IAS figures showed a 23-24 billion forint group net profit for 1996 on 194-195 billion forints operating revenue compared with 3.9 billion profit on 143 billion forints of revenue in 1995.
"We do not want to give figures for Matav Rt, and the group figures are the relevant ones for a possible bourse listing," Straub said.

Matav, Hungary's largest telecommunications company, is 67 percent owned by a 50-50 consortium of Deutsche Telekom and Ameritech and is expected to apply for listing on a foreign bourse in addition to a Budapest bourse listing this year.
So far Matav has said only that it had chosen Merrill Lynch as adviser for a possible IPO.
"We hope to have the company ready for listing by the end of 1997, so we can go as soon as the decisions are taken," Stewart said.
With last year's newly installed capacity the number of Matav's lines has reached 2.1 million and all existing applications will be satisfied by mid-1997, Straub said.
"There will be no more waiting lists," he said. "Hungary's telecommunications system has reached a level where it is no longer an obstacle but rather an incentive for foreign investment".
Another official said Matav was also continuing developments aimed at becoming the region's international telecommunications hub -- an objective set by the state concession.

"By the end of this year we will have 11 optical cable border transits and one microwave link," said Mark von Lillienskold, Matav executive director. He added that the microwave link would be with Bosnia.
Matav has a monopoly on ground-based telephony until December 22, 2001. Last year, however, an OECD report said Hungary should deregulate its telecommunications market before that deadline.
The company would look closely into possibilities of entering the markets of neighbouring countries as a service provider when the opportunity arose, Straub said.
"Although we concentrate on the domestic market, once the opportunity is there we will closely examine it."
He added that they were also considering some involvement in the cable television business.
"It is part of our plans, either by acquiring an existing company or setting up our own one," Straub said.
